questions.text: In REINFORCE, why can a baseline that depends on the state but not the selected action be subtracted from the return?

options.A: It turns the policy update into an exact Bellman optimality backup.
options.B: It removes the need to sample complete trajectories for the update.
options.C: It changes the expected gradient so actions with low return are ignored.
options.D: It can reduce gradient variance without changing the expected gradient.

questions.explanation: An action-independent baseline has zero expected product with the score-function gradient, so subtracting it preserves the expected policy gradient while reducing variance.

questions.text: A REINFORCE agent receives a positive reward early in an episode and a negative reward much later. You want each action update to depend only on rewards that follow that action. Which change should you make?

options.A: Use reward-to-go from each action’s time step as its gradient weight.
options.B: Use the full episode return as the weight for every action in the episode.
options.C: Use only the immediate reward at each step and discard later rewards.
options.D: Use the largest action probability as the weight for every action.

questions.explanation: Reward-to-go weights each log-policy gradient by discounted rewards from that action onward, excluding earlier rewards that the action could not have caused.

questions.text: In reinforce_step, a two-action policy assigns probabilities [0.25, 0.75] and selects action 0. What is grad_log_pi_a immediately after grad_log_pi_a = [-p for p in probs]; grad_log_pi_a[a] += 1.0?
questions.explanation: Negating probabilities gives [-0.25,-0.75]; adding 1 to the chosen action 0 yields [0.75,-0.75].
